LIBRARY API: yes. package.json has main ./dist/lib.js. 'exports' has only an 'import' condition, so it is ESM-only and `require()` won't work. src/lib.ts exports:
- upsertServer(agentType, serverName, McpServerConfig, {local?, cwd?})
- removeServer(...)

These return {success, path, error?} instead of throwing.

CLAUDE CODE: the global target is hard-coded to join(homedir(), '.claude.json') under the top-level 'mcpServers' key (user scope). The entry shape is {type, url, headers, timeout?}. It edits the file directly, not through `claude mcp add`, and ignores CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR.

OPENCODE: the global path is hard-coded to ~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc, or an existing opencode.json. It ignores XDG_CONFIG_HOME.

That keeps comments outside the servers object, but replaces the whole value at the config key (the whole mcpServers / mcp / mcp.servers object), so comments inside that object are lost. If the jsonc edit throws, it falls back to JSON.stringify and every comment is lost.

WRITES: plain fs.writeFileSync. Not atomic, no backup, no lock.

MUSE: not supported. The AgentType union lists 22 agents with no muse, and src/ and README have zero 'muse' matches.

LICENSE: MIT. Version 2.1.2, published 2026-10-19.

FORCING THE BACKEND: pass an options bag as the last constructor argument:
new Entry(service, account, { linux: { store: 'secret-service' } })
This also works for AsyncEntry and Entry.withTarget. The type is LinuxStore = 'secret-service' | 'keyutils'. A pinned store that is unavailable makes the constructor throw, with no fallback.

The README says keyutils is 'completely in-memory and will not persist across reboots'. The code shows this fallback only for 'no Secret Service available'. LINUX BINARY LICENSE: the Linux binaries statically link libdbus (AFL-2.1 OR GPL-2.0-or-later). The notices ship in LICENSE.third-party.md.

checks.evidence: gh api repos/open-mercato/cezar (MIT, 738 stars, pushed 2026-10-20); packages/cezar/src/core/usage-limit.ts (8,521 bytes, read in full); .ai/specs/2026-08-03-auto-resume-after-usage-limit.md (exists, 20,645 bytes)

API: it exports parseUsageLimit(message, now) → {resetAt, evidence} | null, isUsageLimitMessage(), and MAX_USAGE_LIMIT_WAIT_MS (7 days). It parses a run's terminal error string and never throws.

WHAT IT RECOGNIZES, in order:
1. Claude Code's machine-readable 'Claude AI usage limit reached|<epoch seconds>' marker, which comes from an is_error result frame. Milliseconds are tolerated.

checks.claim: (j) Muse Code MCP config: official format of ~/.config/muse/settings.json mcpServers entries (remote HTTP transport name, headers, mode optional/required)
checks.evidence: local: `muse --version` (1.4.11), `muse --help`, `muse config --help`, `muse mcp --help`, `muse mcp login --help`; https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/extending.md; https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/configuration.md; https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/changelog and changelog.md; https://meta-models.github.io/muse-code-sdk/1.4/guides/extend/mcp-servers/ (gh-pages branch of github.com/meta-models/muse-code-sdk, MIT); https://meta-models.github.io/muse-code-sdk/1.4/generated/msp/types/sessionmcpserverconfig/; rulesync src/features/mcp/musecode-mcp.ts
checks.note:
THE OFFICIAL SOURCES DISAGREE.

User manual (dev.meta.ai extending.md):
- Servers go in an 'mcp_servers' block.
- Each has transport 'stdio' (command/args/env) or 'streamable_http' (url/headers), plus enabled and mode.
- mode defaults to 'required'; a required server that fails aborts the whole run. 'optional' skips it with a warning.

Muse SDK developer docs (1.4 guide; the page says its output was produced with Muse 1.3.0):
- 'mcpServers' is canonical.
- type is 'stdio' or 'streamable-http' (hyphen). 'http' is also accepted in settings.json, and type is inferred from url when omitted.
- headers; enabled (default true); boolean 'required', which defaults to FALSE in 1.3.0. The page says this contradicts the manual.
- startup_timeout_sec defaults to 30 and tool_timeout_sec to 300.
- Legacy spellings (mcp_servers, transport:'streamable_http', mode) are accepted in settings.json only.
- A file with BOTH root keys, or a server carrying both a legacy key and its canonical counterpart, disables MCP for the whole session.
- Muse's own settings writes (for example `muse skills disable`) can drop type, cwd, required and timeouts from entries.

configuration.md:
- The file is ~/.config/muse/settings.json (the SDK docs say $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/muse/settings.json).
- It must contain "schema_version": 1, or every command fails with 'malformed settings file'. A missing file is fine.

Changelog:
- 0.2.1: 'Settings accept the standard mcpServers key'.
- 1.4.4: MCP server url and header values in settings.json and a trusted project .mcp.json expand ${VAR} and ${VAR:-default} ($$ for a literal $). The 1.3.0-based SDK page says headers are literal, so this changed in 1.4.4.

Local 1.4.11 help: '<server> is a streamable-HTTP entry under mcpServers in settings.json'.

Safest entry (untested): use whichever root key already exists and never add the second. Use url + headers, with exactly one explicit optional flag: "required": false or the legacy "mode": "optional", never both. Write "schema_version": 1 when creating the file.

extra_findings: Muse can get MCP servers per run or per session, so editing its global settings.json can be avoided. (1) Since 1.4.4, repeatable `-c key=value` on the TUI, exec and serve 'set any existing setting for that run only, including MCP servers; secret fields take ${VAR} references'. The exact key path for adding one server entry is NOT verified. (2) `muse serve` (the session protocol) takes per-session SessionMcpServerConfig {transport:'streamableHttp', url, headers, mode (default required)} at session start. The TypeScript SDK @muse-code/sdk 1.4.11 (MIT, on npm) wraps that protocol. (3) Since 1.4.0, a trusted project .mcp.json in Claude's format ('type':'http' accepted) overrides user settings. Together with Claude's --mcp-config and OpenCode's OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT, the desktop app could inject the hub at launch for all three CLIs, as Parallel Code already does for its own server, instead of writing global configs. Caveat: issue meta-models/muse-code-sdk#65 (2026-09-29) reported that 1.4.1 had no per-run MCP flag and did not load a project .mcp.json.

OpenCode v2 native MCP shape (opencode.ai/v2/docs/mcp-servers and v2.opencode.ai migrate-v1): mcp.servers.<name> = {type:'remote', url, headers, oauth (set false for API-key-header servers), disabled (replaces enabled), codemode (default true, so tools go through Code Mode), timeout:{catalog,execution}, protocol: 'legacy' (default) | 'auto' | '2026-07-28'}. Secrets use {env:NAME} substitution. The V1 shape outside the three breaking areas is 'intended to remain compatible'. design.md D6 currently says `mcp.hub` with type remote, which is the V1 shape. The local ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json already contains a 'servers' key, so add-mcp would write V2 there.

Protocol eras: MCP spec 2026-07-28 is the 'modern' era (server/discover, stateless HTTP, a _meta envelope on every request). The 'legacy' era (2024-10-07 to 2025-11-25) uses initialize. Muse advertises 2025-06-18 (changelog 1.2.1) and OpenCode v2 defaults to protocol 'legacy', so the hub's downstream endpoint must speak the legacy era. In SDK v2, createMcpHandler serves both eras from one endpoint, and its client can use versionNegotiation 'auto' toward upstream providers.

Licensing: the MCP SDK v2 split packages, add-mcp, 1MCP and Waybill are all Apache-2.0. The v1 @modelcontextprotocol/sdk, @napi-rs/keyring, rulesync, cli-continues, cezar, session-migrate and @muse-code/sdk are MIT. Depending on Apache-2.0 packages is fine for an MIT app, but copied or bundled code must keep their license text. The @napi-rs/keyring Linux binary statically links libdbus (AFL-2.1 OR GPL-2.0-or-later), so a packaged .rpm or AppImage should ship its LICENSE.third-party.md.

add-mcp falls short of design.md D6 as an adapter dependency. It is ESM-only and does non-atomic writeFileSync with no backup or lock. It hard-codes ~/.claude.json and ~/.config/opencode, ignoring CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR and XDG_CONFIG_HOME, and writes ~/.claude.json directly instead of through `claude mcp add`. On an empty OpenCode config it writes the V1 shape, it loses comments inside the servers object, and it has no Muse support. D6 asks for atomic rename, backups, a no-op compare and the Claude CLI where possible. Using add-mcp means wrapping it with backup and atomic logic, or reimplementing the roughly 150 relevant lines on jsonc-parser.

Port only the field mapping from rulesync's Muse writer, not its write strategy. It replaces the whole servers block, ignores XDG_CONFIG_HOME, and when a file has both root keys it writes mcp_servers. Per the Muse SDK docs, a file with both keys disables MCP for that session.

cli-continues may not work here as a handoff dependency. It has had no commits since 2026-05-07. Its OpenCode parser targets the v1 SQLite schema, which doesn't match the local OpenCode v2.0.32 database. It needs Node >=22.5 for node:sqlite; whether Electron's bundled Node exposes node:sqlite was not verified.

@napi-rs/keyring decides the store each time an Entry is created when no option is given. If the Secret Service is briefly unavailable, one write can silently land in in-memory keyutils and later reads will miss it. Always construct with {linux:{store:'secret-service'}} and show a clear error when that throws.

Possible 1MCP engine path: 1MCP is CLI-only, so the app would spawn `1mcp serve`. Its header values support ${VAR} resolved from the parent environment, so a parent process could pass keyring-sourced env vars and keep keys off disk. This is inferred from the docs, not tested. 1MCP's inbound (client-facing) auth model was not re-verified in this pass.

Muse 1.4.11's local data directory has a top-level ~/.local/share/muse/session-index.db alongside the YYYY/MM/DD/<uuid>/session.jsonl directories. session-migrate's format doc is pinned to Muse 0.2.1, so a Muse handoff reader must be re-validated against 1.4.x.

cezar's limit detector works on a captured terminal error string, such as Claude's headless is_error result frame with 'Claude AI usage limit reached|<epoch>'. Interactive TUI sessions don't produce that, so the Claude statusline rate_limits that Parallel Code already parses remain the better live signal there.

Muse's settings.json is fragile for a global-config adapter. Unknown top-level members are reported at startup, a missing schema_version breaks every command, two root keys disable MCP, and Muse's own settings writes can strip fields from entries. Per-launch injection, or `doctor` re-checking the entry after each Muse settings write, reduces that risk.

checks.claim: (b) Parallel Code passes '--mcp-config' to OpenCode and to custom agents
checks.evidence: electron/mcp/canvas-config.ts canConfigureCanvasMcp; src/store/delegation.ts isSupportedDelegationAgent (L289-291); src/components/NewTaskPanel.tsx orchestrationEnabled (~L443-451); electron/mcp/delegation.ts (~L410-414); electron/ipc/register.ts SpawnAgent handler (~L664-806); PR johannesjo/parallel-code#248 body
checks.note: Every MCP injection path only runs when the command's basename is claude, codex or copilot: canvas tools check canConfigureCanvasMcp, coordinator mode checks isSupportedDelegationAgent (the New Task panel hides orchestration for other agents), and delegated children throw 'Select a supported agent without custom MCP configuration'. So OpenCode and custom agents (Muse included) currently launch with no Parallel Code MCP args at all. checks.claim: (b) Parallel Code injects MCP only when orchestration/delegation is on
checks.evidence: src/components/TerminalView.tsx (~L1214-1226, canvasMcp flag); electron/ipc/register.ts SpawnAgent (~L709-806); electron/ipc/mcp-runtime.ts restoreOrchestrationEnabled (L49-59); src/store/core.ts (mcpOrchestrationEnabled: true); gh code search 'strict-mcp-config'
checks.note: There are two layers. (1) Canvas/session MCP: the renderer sends canvasMcp=true for every task that is not in coordinatorMode and not coordinatedBy another task. The main process then injects the parallel-code server on every fresh, non-shell spawn of claude, codex or copilot, as long as the agent's own args have no --mcp-config, --additional-mcp-config, --strict-mcp-config or codex mcp_servers override. This doesn't depend on the orchestration toggle. If setup fails, the agent starts without canvas tools. (2) Coordinator MCP: only for coordinator tasks and their children, which needs the mcpOrchestrationEnabled setting (default true), worktree isolation and a supported agent. Parallel Code never sends --strict-mcp-config. What this means for the hub: putting a hub --mcp-config into an agent's args turns off Parallel Code's canvas tools for that launch, and for managed children it throws 'Custom MCP configuration cannot be replaced automatically'. The hook should go in the main process, in electron/ipc/pty.ts spawnAgent next to applyAgentHookLaunch. Both the IPC SpawnAgent handler and coordinator.ts sub-task spawns go through that function.

checks.claim: (c) electron/ipc/env-file.ts loads a per-project .env into agent PTYs
checks.evidence: electron/ipc/env-file.ts; src/components/AgentEnvFileEditor.tsx; src/store/agents.ts setAgentEnvFile; electron/ipc/pty.ts (ENV_BLOCK_LIST ~L263-322, buildPtySpawnEnv ~L429-451, loadEnvFile call ~L807); src/store/tasks.ts (StartMCPServer agentEnvFile)
checks.note: It loads a KEY=VALUE file into agent PTYs, but per AGENT, not per project. The user picks the file path per agent in Settings (store.agentEnvFiles[agentId]), for built-in and custom agents alike. Rules: the path must be absolute or start with ~/, it must be a regular file of at most 256 KiB, and it is parsed with Node's util.parseEnv. A missing or unreadable file fails the spawn instead of silently continuing. The file is re-read on every spawn. Everything is filtered through ENV_BLOCK_LIST: PATH, HOME, USER, SHELL, LD_*, DYLD_*, NODE_OPTIONS, NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS, NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED, BASH_ENV, ENV, GIT_SSH_COMMAND and the GIT_CONFIG_* overrides, PERL/RUBY/PYTHON path vars, ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE, PARALLEL_CODE_MCP_TOKEN and DOCKER_*. checks.claim: (g) Claude Code '--mcp-config' accepts files and/or JSON strings, and '--strict-mcp-config' limits a session to them
checks.evidence: local `claude --help`; https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference
checks.note: `--mcp-config <configs...>` is documented as "Load MCP servers from JSON files or strings (space-separated)". With -p, it waits for pending servers up to MCP_TIMEOUT (30 s by default). `--strict-mcp-config` uses only the servers from --mcp-config; without it, the other scopes still load. Not tested: whether two separate --mcp-config flags add up (this one also gets Parallel Code's canvas config), so the safe move is to put both values after a single flag. checks.claim: (g) Claude Code expands ${VAR} references inside the headers of configs passed with --mcp-config
checks.evidence: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp (sections: Environment variable expansion in .mcp.json; Credential variables that read as empty; headersHelper; Where the helper runs; Which variables a helper can read)
checks.note: The docs cover ${VAR} and ${VAR:-default} expansion for .mcp.json, in command, args, env, url and headers. An unset variable without a default stays as literal text and shows a warning. In remote url and headers, credential names read as empty: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK, HTTPS_PROXY, NPM_TOKEN and similar. Other names expand normally. The docs never say whether --mcp-config configs get the same expansion, and I couldn't test it (only --help was allowed). A documented alternative does cover --mcp-config: `headersHelper`, a shell command that prints a JSON object of headers. It runs at session start and on reconnect, has a 10 s limit, re-runs after a 401/403 and overrides static headers. For --mcp-config servers it runs in the session's main working directory and keeps the credential env vars. That would let the hub token stay in the keyring and never be written to a file.

checks.claim: (g) OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT is inline JSON config with the highest runtime precedence
checks.evidence: https://opencode.ai/docs/config; anomalyco/opencode@dev: packages/core/src/config.ts, packages/cli/src/server-process.ts, packages/cli/src/services/standalone.ts, packages/cli/src/services/server-connection.ts, packages/cli/src/services/service-config.ts; local `opencode --help`
checks.note: Load order, later wins: remote .well-known config, global ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json, OPENCODE_CONFIG, project opencode.json, .opencode dirs, OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT ("runtime overrides"), managed files (/etc/opencode on Linux), macOS MDM. So it is the strongest layer a user controls, but managed config still beats it. Layers merge by key; they don't replace each other. Important for v2: the SERVER process reads this variable. By default the TUI attaches to a shared background service, unless you pass `--standalone` or service.json has disabled:true. Only standalone mode spawns a private `opencode serve --stdio --port 0` with extendEnv:true, so only then does a per-launch env var take effect. The shared service has one global env map in service.json. Parallel Code's opencode preset passes no args, so no --standalone.

checks.claim: (g) OpenCode v2 config uses 'mcp.servers.<name>' (v1 used 'mcp.<name>')
checks.evidence: https://opencode.ai/config.json; anomalyco/opencode@dev: packages/schema/src/config/mcp.ts, packages/schema/src/mcp.ts (RemoteConfig), packages/core/src/config/normalize.ts; https://opencode.ai/docs/mcp-servers
checks.note: The v2 native shape is mcp: { timeout?: {startup, catalog, execution}, servers: { <name>: { type: "remote", url, headers?, oauth?: {...}|false, disabled?, codemode?, timeout?, protocol? } } }. codemode defaults to true, which exposes the server's tools through Code Mode. protocol is "legacy" (default), "auto" or "2026-07-28". The v1 shape mcp.<name> {type, url, enabled, headers, oauth, timeout in ms} is still accepted and converted into servers. The names 'servers' and 'timeout' are reserved, and entries with only `enabled` are dropped. The public docs pages still show only the v1 shape.

The 1.4.4 changelog says exec, the TUI and serve accept repeatable -c key=value flags that "set any existing setting for that run only, including MCP servers; secret fields take ${VAR} references instead of inline values and managed policy still wins." If they do, the whole header value must be one variable, e.g. "Authorization": "${HUB_AUTH}" with HUB_AUTH="Bearer <token>", not "Bearer ${HUB_TOKEN}". This needs a hands-on test.

checks.claim: Existing design D6: Muse Code reads MCP servers from ~/.config/muse/settings.json under 'mcpServers'
checks.evidence: https://meta-models.github.io/muse-code-sdk/next/guides/extend/mcp-servers (dated 2026-10-02, describes 1.3.0); https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/extending; https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/configuration; https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/changelog
checks.note: The file is right. The SDK docs make `mcpServers` the canonical key, with type "stdio" or "streamable-http" ("http" also accepted), url, headers, enabled, required (default false) and startup/tool timeouts. Meta's user manual uses the older spellings: `mcp_servers`, transport "streamable_http" and mode, and says mode defaults to required, which aborts the run if the server fails. Both spellings work in settings.json, but a file with both root keys, or a server with both type and transport (or required and mode), turns off ALL MCP for that session. settings.json must contain "schema_version": 1, or every command fails. Header ${VAR}/${VAR:-default} expansion only exists since 1.4.4 (the SDK page says headers are literal in 1.3.0). Commands that save settings can rewrite the file and drop fields such as required, cwd, type and timeouts. A trusted project .mcp.json (canonical names only) overrides user settings. Muse reads MCP config once per process, and tools are named mcp__<server>__<tool>.

extra_findings: Stage 1 (global sync) works with an unmodified Parallel Code. It never passes --strict-mcp-config, it gives Claude its own canvas config as an extra --mcp-config file, and it gives OpenCode and custom agents no MCP args at all. So hub entries synced into ~/.claude.json, ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json and ~/.config/muse/settings.json still load in sessions it launches. Per-launch injection can wait.

Don't inject the hub through agent preset args for claude, codex or copilot. Any MCP flag in the args makes Parallel Code skip its own canvas/session MCP, and managed coordinator children then fail with 'Custom MCP configuration cannot be replaced automatically'. Inject from the main process in electron/ipc/pty.ts spawnAgent, after those checks, or add a 'hub' entry to the 0600 config file Parallel Code already writes (canvas: os.tmpdir()/parallel-code-canvas-<agentId>.json, deleted when the PTY exits).

There are three launch paths to cover. (1) PTY: pty.ts spawnAgent, used by the renderer's SpawnAgent IPC and by coordinator sub-tasks. (2) Claude chat view: electron/chat/claude.ts uses @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk query() with extraArgs {'mcp-config': <one file>}. (3) Codex chat: the Codex app-server. Docker-mode tasks run in containers, where the host's 127.0.0.1 isn't reachable (Parallel Code uses a wide bind for its own server there), so a loopback-only hub would not serve Docker tasks. That last point is inferred from register.ts and canvas-config.ts.

Parallel Code already depends on @modelcontextprotocol/sdk (1.32.1 locked) and bundles its own MCP server with esbuild into dist-electron/mcp-server.cjs (asarUnpack). A TypeScript hub can reuse the same toolchain and bundling. Its own remote/MCP server uses port 7777 when packaged and 8777 in dev, so the hub's default 7337 doesn't collide.

Parallel Code already has a cross-agent 'second opinion' handoff (src/lib/agent-handoff.ts, src/components/AgentHandoffComposer.tsx, added 2026-10-09 to 10-11) plus peer messaging between panes in the same worktree. That's a natural starting point for the planned 'Continue in…' handoff. It also already ships an OpenCode preset, and Muse can run as a custom agent with a wrapper script, so the presets alone may not need a fork.

OpenCode v2: per-launch env injection (OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT) needs `opencode --standalone`, or disabled:true in OpenCode's service.json. Otherwise the TUI talks to a shared background service whose env was fixed when it started. Also, codemode defaults to true, so MCP tools are exposed through Code Mode instead of as direct tools. Test the hub's prefixed tool names under Code Mode, or set codemode:false on the hub entry.

Muse adapter pitfalls: keep whichever root key the user's file already uses, because adding the other one (mcpServers vs mcp_servers) silently turns off all MCP. Always write "schema_version": 1. Set required:false or mode:'optional' explicitly, since the docs disagree on the default. Re-check the entry after Muse rewrites settings. Since -c refuses 'clashing keys', choose one mechanism per CLI: global settings entry or per-run -c, not both.

Claude: give the hub token a custom variable name, not one Claude treats as a credential (ANTHROPIC_*, NPM_TOKEN-style names on its list). Better still, use headersHelper, so the token is never written into any config file or argv.

A third-party issue (meta-models/muse-code-sdk#45, 2026-09-25) reports that `muse serve` (the MSP protocol) accepts per-session MCP servers via session/start.config.mcpServers (capability sessionMcp). That would be a clean per-session route if the app ever drives Muse over MSP instead of a PTY. I haven't confirmed it in Meta's official docs.

Upstreaming risk: a new agent preset with MCP integration gets long, multi-round reviews (#248, the Kimi Code preset, open about 3 months), and the rpm PR #315 is unreviewed. Plan to carry Fedora rpm packaging and any Muse or hub hooks as small fork patches in new files, with thin hooks, and offer them upstream in small pieces.

On a fresh Fedora machine, building needs a C++ compiler, make and python3, because node-pty has no linux-x64 prebuild. Installing needs either an rpm target (PR #315) or the AppImage, since upstream install.sh uses dpkg. Node must be >= 22.12.
